screens.title: Advanced Troubleshooting with Network Access Analyzer and Reachability Analyzer
screens.narratorSegment: In complex AWS networks, answering whether a path exists or whether an unintended path can reach a resource should be definitive and repeatable. This lesson introduces two AWS analysis tools that move beyond logs and manual checks. First, Network Access Analyzer lets you define an access scope—an origin, a destination, and optional intermediate components—and then it inspects security groups, NACLs, route tables, and gateways to report any potential paths that violate your scope. This is essential for proactive auditing and compliance. Second, Reachability Analyzer accepts a specific source and destination, plus protocol and port, and simulates the virtual network path to say whether the route is reachable and, if not, which component blocks it. Throughout this chapter you will see concrete examples, a CLI walkthrough for Reachability Analyzer, a hands-on lab to practice, and common mistakes to avoid such as relying on static analysis as if it were real-time traffic. By the end, you will know when to use each tool, how to interpret the findings, and how these tools reduce guesswork when troubleshooting multi-VPC and hybrid scenarios. Consider a recent connectivity issue you faced and how a static path analysis might have saved time.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Advanced Troubleshooting

Advanced Troubleshooting

Network Access Analyzer • Reachability Analyzer
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

This chapter teaches two complementary AWS tools. Network Access Analyzer finds unintended potential paths by evaluating configuration state against a defined scope. Reachability Analyzer traces a specific path between a source and destination to confirm connectivity and locate the blocking component. Both are static, configuration-based analyses that reduce manual checks.

You will learn how to define scopes, run point-to-point analyses, interpret the explanation output, and apply findings to remediate misconfigurations in multi-VPC, Transit Gateway, and hybrid environments.

Explore Key Topics
Network Access Analyzer
Define access scopes to proactively audit configuration for unintended paths.
Reachability Analyzer
Trace a virtual path between two resources to see hop-by-hop results and blocking components.
Interpretation & Remediation
Translate analyzer findings into targeted changes: SG rules, routes, or NACL entries.
Visual concept
Scope-based audit
Define allowed origins and destinations; analyzer reports any matching paths.
Point-to-point trace
Simulate a path and find the exact hop that blocks traffic.
Remediation
Use findings to change security group rules, routes, or NACLs precisely.
Coming up: definitions, CLI walkthrough, a hands-on lab, and common pitfalls.

First, you'll use Network Access Analyzer to audit network configurations against explicit access requirements. That means you will learn to define an access scope—an origin, destination, and optional intermediates—and interpret the analyzer's reported paths to detect unintended exposure. Second, you'll employ Reachability Analyzer to diagnose point-to-point connectivity problems. You'll learn to create a path analysis with the correct source and destination identifiers, choose protocol and port, and read the hop-by-hop results to identify blocking components. Both objectives focus on turning configuration state into actionable troubleshooting data rather than guessing from logs. Each objective includes a short practical checkpoint so you can verify competency: design a scope for a production subnet and run a basic reachability path between two ENIs. These skills are directly useful when operating multi-VPC, Transit Gateway, VPN, or Direct Connect networks where manual verification is time-consuming and error-prone.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Interpretation
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide focuses on practice and interpretation. You will run a Reachability Analyzer path and read the explanation field to identify the exact blocking rule—this trains you to convert analyzer output to a remediation plan. You will also define at least one Network Access Analyzer scope to capture a real compliance requirement, for example preventing internet access to a production database subnet. Practically, this means setting an origin of '0.0.0.0/0' or 'All internet' and a destination subnet, then reviewing reported paths. Finally, you will learn to check IAM and cost implications before automating analyses. These steps are not theoretical: they prepare you to audit live environments and resolve connectivity failures faster than manual inspection. A common misconception we correct here is treating these tools as real-time traffic monitors—they analyze configuration state, not transient packets. That distinction guides when to use flow logs versus when to run a scope or path analysis.

screens.title: Why manual network troubleshooting is fragile
screens.narratorSegment: When networks grow beyond a single VPC, manual troubleshooting becomes slow and error-prone. There are multiple places where access can be allowed or denied: security groups attached to ENIs, stateless NACLs on subnets, route table entries that forward traffic to an internet gateway, NAT gateway, or Transit Gateway, and peering or VPN links that connect networks. Each of these components must be examined and understood together. The problem is combinatorial: a single missing route or an overly broad security group can create either a silent failure or an unintended open path. Network Access Analyzer and Reachability Analyzer address different parts of this problem. Network Access Analyzer treats configuration as a whole and asks: given these current rules and routes, are there any potential paths that violate my policy? Reachability Analyzer answers a narrower question: given a source and destination, is there a path, and if not, which specific hop denies or lacks a rule? A common misconception is to rely only on flow logs or manual checks; flow logs show what happened, which is useful, but they may not reveal a potential misconfiguration that hasn't yet resulted in traffic. Translating debugging into declarative analysis lets you find issues earlier and with less guesswork. Think of manual checks as reading the symptoms, while these tools read the system's design and identify both symptoms and latent risks.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Why manual troubleshooting is fragile
Definition
Large AWS networks include many layers that influence connectivity: security groups, stateless NACLs, route tables, gateways, peering, Transit Gateways, and VPN/Direct Connect. Manually checking each layer is slow and can miss interactions between components. Declarative analysis examines configuration state holistically and finds potential access paths without waiting for traffic to occur.
Common failure points
  • Missing or incorrect route table entry.
  • Security group lacking an inbound or outbound rule.
  • Stateless NACL denying traffic in one direction.
  • Transit Gateway or peering not propagating routes as expected.
Analogy
Think of manual checks as inspecting street signs one at a time. An automated analyzer reads every sign and simulates every possible route to see if an unintended path exists.
Key Takeaway

Use configuration-based tools to find latent paths and reduce manual inspection time.

Concrete example
Imagine two subnets in different VPCs connected by a Transit Gateway. A missing route in one route table prevents traffic, but a permissive security group elsewhere could allow unexpected access from another VPC. A manual engineer might check security groups first, miss the route problem, and waste time. An analyzer will show both potential and actual blocking points for the same configuration snapshot.
Check your understanding
List the three most likely components to inspect when two EC2 instances cannot communicate and explain which analyzer helps you confirm each component's effect.

screens.title: Network Access Analyzer — purpose and workflow
screens.narratorSegment: Network Access Analyzer inspects your network configuration to reveal potential paths that match a defined access scope. An access scope expresses the origin and destination you care about, plus optional intermediate constraints. For example, you might assert that ‘no internet access exists to production database subnets’ or that ‘only the management VPC may reach application management ports’. The analyzer then looks across security groups, NACLs, route tables, internet and NAT gateways, VPC peering, and Transit Gateways to enumerate any paths that would satisfy that scope. This is especially useful for compliance: rather than searching logs for traffic that happened, you check whether a configuration allows traffic at all. The workflow is: define scope, run analysis, review reported paths, and remediate misconfigurations. A common misconception is thinking the analyzer verifies live traffic; it does not. It reports potential paths based on current configuration. Use it to find latent exposures and to validate design constraints. As a concrete example, define a scope with origin: anywhere on the internet, destination: your DB subnet. If the analyzer reports a path, it will highlight the component—perhaps a route through an internet gateway combined with a permissive security group—that creates the exposure.

keyIdea.text: Network Access Analyzer checks configuration state against a declared access scope to find any potential paths that violate policy.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Network Access Analyzer
Purpose
Network Access Analyzer helps you define and prove security constraints by evaluating configuration state. It reports any potential network paths that match your scope so you can remediate unintended access before it becomes an incident.
Access Scope
A declarative origin and destination with optional intermediate components used to filter and find relevant paths.
Analysis output
A list of matching paths and the components that form them so you can identify exposures or confirm compliance.
Key Takeaway

Use Network Access Analyzer to proactively verify that your configuration does not permit disallowed paths.

Concrete example
Define a scope: origin = internet (0.0.0.0/0), destination = production DB subnet. Run analysis. If the analyzer returns a path, it will show the route plus a security group allowing inbound traffic, or a NAT/IGW combo that enables the path. That single report points to precise remediation.
Misconception check
This is not a live traffic monitor. If no traffic has occurred, Network Access Analyzer can still find a path that would allow traffic if attempted.

screens.title: Access Scope: define, refine, and run
screens.narratorSegment: An access scope is the most important input to a Network Access Analyzer audit. Think of the scope as a filter that limits analysis to the traffic you care about. Start by choosing a clear origin: it can be an IP range, 'anywhere on the internet', or a specific VPC or subnet. Next, choose a precise destination: for compliance you might select a database subnet, specific ENIs, or a service endpoint. Optionally include intermediates such as Transit Gateways or specific VPC peering connections to narrow results. After you define the scope, run the analysis and inspect any returned paths. If you see many results, refine the scope—narrow the origin, constrain protocols or ports, or add an intermediate—to reduce noise. A practical example: to verify no internet access to your production DB subnet, set origin to the internet and destination to the DB subnet, then run analysis. If the analyzer finds a path, the report will show which combination of route entries and security group rules permit that path. Misdefining a scope is a common source of false negatives or noisy outputs; take time to iterate. The goal is to produce a focused report that directly points to misconfigurations you can fix.

keyIdea.title: Scope tip
keyIdea.text: Define a focused scope and iterate—narrow origins, destinations, and intermediates to reduce noise and reveal actionable paths.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Access Scope
Process
Follow a short process to get meaningful results from Network Access Analyzer: choose origin, choose destination, optionally add intermediates or protocol constraints, run the analysis, then refine the scope if output is noisy.
Step 1: Origin
Pick exactly where traffic starts: an IP range, VPC, or the internet.
Step 2: Destination
Select targeted resources like a subnet or ENIs for focused auditing.
Step 3: Intermediates
Optionally lock in components such as Transit Gateway or peering to limit paths considered.
Example
Origin = 0.0.0.0/0, Destination = production-db-subnet. Run analysis. If paths appear, inspect the listed route entries and security groups to see how exposure occurs.
Refinement
If you get too many paths, restrict by protocol, add an intermediate, or narrow the IP range to eliminate noise.

screens.title: Reachability Analyzer — purpose and capabilities
screens.narratorSegment: Reachability Analyzer is designed for targeted troubleshooting: when you have a specific source and destination and want to know definitively whether a path exists and why. You provide the source and destination—these can be ENIs, IP addresses, or service endpoints—and optionally specify a protocol and destination port. The analyzer performs a static simulation of the virtual network path and returns either a reachable result or an explanation that identifies the blocking component. The value is precision: if the path is unreachable, the analysis tells you if a security group denied traffic, a route entry is missing, or a NACL blocks return traffic. Use it when two resources fail to communicate and you want to remove guesswork. A common use case is two EC2 instances in different subnets that cannot ping each other. Rather than manually examining every security group and route table, create a Reachability path and read the explanation. Remember that Reachability Analyzer works from the current configuration snapshot; if you modify rules after running an analysis, rerun to refresh results. This tool reduces troubleshooting time by directly mapping symptoms to a configuration-level cause.

keyIdea.title: What it does
keyIdea.text: Reachability Analyzer simulates a path between a specific source and destination and points to the hop that allows or blocks traffic.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Reachability Analyzer
Purpose
Reachability Analyzer answers: does a path exist between these two endpoints, and if not, which component blocks traffic? It examines the same network components as Network Access Analyzer but focuses on a single point-to-point path and produces a hop-by-hop explanation.
Inputs
Source and destination (ENIs or IPs), optional protocol and port, and descriptive path name.
Output
Reachable: Yes/No and a detailed explanation listing each hop and the acceptance or denial reason.
Key Takeaway

Use Reachability Analyzer when you need a definitive, hop-by-hop diagnosis of a specific connectivity failure.

Concrete example
If two EC2 instances in different subnets cannot ping, create a Reachability path with their ENIs and protocol ICMP. When the analysis completes, you'll see 'Reachable: No' with an explanation like 'Security group sg-012... denied ICMP from 10.0.1.10 to 10.0.2.20'. That message tells you exactly which security group rule to change.
Misconception check
Reachability Analyzer does not generate or capture live packets. It evaluates current configuration to determine whether a virtual path exists.

screens.title: CLI example: creating a Reachability Analyzer path
screens.narratorSegment: The Reachability Analyzer can be invoked from the AWS CLI, which is useful for automating diagnostics or integrating with runbooks. The CLI flow typically creates a network-insights-path, starts an analysis, and then describes the analysis result. The create step requires a source IP or ENI ARN and a destination IP or ENI ARN, plus protocol and destination port when relevant. After you create the path, start the analysis and poll describe-network-insights-analyses until it reports success. The analysis output includes an Explanation field that states whether the path is reachable and, if not, precisely why. A concrete CLI example is included visually on this slide—use it as a pattern but replace ENI ARNs and IPs with your actual values. Remember IAM permissions: the calling principal needs CreateNetworkInsightsPath and Start/Describe permissions for the relevant resources. Also remember to re-run analyses after configuration changes to keep results current. A common mistake is reading the CLI output without checking the Explanation: that field is the actionable part that points to the blocking component. CLI example: creating a Reachability Analyzer path means create a path, start an analysis, and describe the analysis to read the explanation field for the blocking cause.. In practical terms, step through the aws cli commands to create and analyze a network-insights path. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › CLI: Reachability Analyzer
Commands (example)
Replace ENI ARNs, IPs, and IDs with your environment values. This sequence creates a path, starts analysis, and retrieves results.
# Create the path
aws ec2 create-network-insights-path \
    --source-ip 10.0.1.10 \
    --destination-ip 10.0.2.20 \
    --protocol tcp \
    --destination-port 80 \
    --source-arn arn:aws:ec2:us-east-1:123456789012:network-interface/eni-0abcdef1234567890 \
    --destination-arn arn:aws:ec2:us-east-1:123456789012:network-interface/eni-0fedcba9876543210

# Note the returned NetworkInsightsPathId (nip-...)

# Start the analysis
aws ec2 start-network-insights-analysis \
    --network-insights-path-id nip-0123456789abcdef0

# Check status until it's 'succeeded'
aws ec2 describe-network-insights-analyses \
    --network-insights-analysis-ids nia-0fedcba9876543210
The describe output contains an Explanation field that identifies whether the path is reachable and, if not, which component denied traffic.
Concrete CLI guidance
  • Use ENI ARNs for accuracy when possible.
  • Include protocol and port to narrow analysis.
  • Poll describe until analysis completes before reading Explanation.
Key Takeaway

Use the Explanation field as the primary actionable output when using the CLI.

screens.title: Interpreting Reachability Analyzer results
screens.narratorSegment: The most valuable output from Reachability Analyzer is the hop-by-hop Explanation. It lists each virtual hop—source ENI, security groups, route table decisions, Transit Gateway attachments, NACL evaluations—and shows whether the hop accepted or denied traffic. When the analysis reports Reachable: Yes, you have verification that a path exists under current configuration. When it reports Reachable: No, examine the first denial in the explanation: it typically names the component and why it denied traffic, such as a security group without an inbound rule or a missing route entry. Translate that message into a remediation: add or adjust a security group rule, create or update a route table entry, or correct a NACL entry. Also verify return path symmetry: some components are stateful and some are not—if return traffic is blocked by a NACL, the forward path might appear allowed but the traffic still fails. A common misconception is assuming a reachability 'No' always points to a security group; the explanation may show a route or a missing Transit Gateway attachment instead. Use the explanation as your single source of truth when mapping to remediation.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Interpreting Results
Hop-by-hop explanation
The Explanation lists each hop and whether it accepted or denied traffic, with a reason for denials. Your first action is to find the earliest hop that denies traffic—this is usually the most direct place to remediate.
Example explanation snippet
"Security group sg-012... denied traffic from 10.0.1.10 to 10.0.2.20 on port 80" — change the SG inbound rule or reference the caller's SG.
Return path symmetry
Verify both forward and return path rules. NACLs are stateless and require mirrored entries for both directions; security groups are stateful.
Key Takeaway

Act on the first denying hop reported. Check return path symmetry to avoid partial fixes.

  • Security group missing inbound/outbound rule.
  • Route table missing an entry to the destination.
  • NACL denies traffic on one direction.
  • Transit Gateway attachment not present or not propagating.
Pro tip: after making a change, rerun the analysis to confirm Reachable: Yes rather than assuming the fix worked.

screens.title: Network Access Analyzer vs Reachability Analyzer
screens.narratorSegment: These two tools solve different troubleshooting classes. Use Network Access Analyzer when you need a proactive, policy-driven audit across your network: define an access scope and find any potential paths that violate your requirements. It's best for compliance checks, audit runs, and broad validation across VPCs, Transit Gateways, and service endpoints. Reachability Analyzer is for targeted troubleshooting: when a specific connection fails, specify source and destination and get a hop-by-hop explanation that points to the blocking configuration. A helpful way to think about their difference is breadth versus depth—Network Access Analyzer covers broad surface area for unintended paths; Reachability Analyzer dives deep for one path and gives granular denial reasons. They complement each other: you might use Network Access Analyzer to find an exposure at scale, then use Reachability Analyzer to debug a particular affected pair. A common misconception is that one supersedes the other; they solve related but distinct problems and are often used together in a remediation workflow. Consider automating periodic Network Access Analyzer checks for compliance and using Reachability Analyzer in your incident runbook for targeted diagnostics.

screens.title: Lab walkthrough: Diagnose a ping failure with Reachability Analyzer
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on lab walks you through a common scenario: two EC2 instances initially communicate, then a security group change blocks ICMP and you use Reachability Analyzer to diagnose the cause. Start with two EC2 instances in the same VPC but different subnets. Verify initial connectivity by pinging the destination from the source instance. Next, edit the destination's security group and remove the inbound ICMP rule that allowed the source. Confirm the ping now fails. In the VPC console open Reachability Analyzer and create a path: choose the source ENI and destination ENI, set protocol to ICMP, and run the analysis. When completed, the analysis should show Reachable: No with an Explanation that names the security group denying ICMP. Remediate by re-adding the inbound ICMP rule referencing the source's security group, then run the analysis again. You should now see Reachable: Yes and the ping will succeed. This exercise demonstrates how Reachability Analyzer maps the symptom to the exact blocking component and shortens the repair loop compared to manual rule inspection. screens.title: Permissions, cost, and safety considerations
screens.narratorSegment: Before automating or delegating analyses, understand permissions, cost, and when to rerun checks. IAM: the principal performing analyses must have ec2:CreateNetworkInsightsPath, ec2:StartNetworkInsightsAnalysis, and ec2:Describe* permissions for the relevant resources. Apply least privilege—do not give broader rights than required for analysis. Cost: analyses are billed; be mindful when scheduling frequent automated runs—limit scope and frequency to balance assurance and cost. Safety: both tools perform read-only, static evaluations and do not change network configuration. That said, stale analysis results are a risk: if you change a security group or route after running an analysis, the prior result is no longer authoritative. Always rerun analyses after making configuration changes. Using all three gives a robust troubleshooting and audit capability without over-relying on any single data source. screens.title: Best practices and common mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Adopt a few best practices to make Network Access Analyzer and Reachability Analyzer effective parts of your network operations. First, be precise in scope definitions to reduce noise in Network Access Analyzer reports; iterative refinement yields actionable output. Second, use ENI identifiers for Reachability Analyzer when possible to avoid ambiguity introduced by changing IPs. Third, always check the Explanation field—it's the most actionable element and explicitly identifies the blocking component. Fourth, make analysis results part of your runbook: when an alarm fires, run a targeted Reachability analysis as a diagnostic step. Common mistakes include treating these tools as real-time traffic monitors, over-automating analyses without permission limits or cost controls, and failing to rerun analyses after configuration changes. Also avoid assuming the first reported path is the only important one; check whether multiple paths exist that could create exposure. Finally, combine findings with flow logs and CloudTrail records when validating an incident to ensure that both configuration and actual traffic behavior align. These practices will reduce mean time to repair and improve security posture. fullNarratorScript:
In complex AWS networks, answering whether a path exists or whether an unintended path can reach a resource should be definitive and repeatable. This lesson introduces two AWS analysis tools that move beyond logs and manual checks. First, Network Access Analyzer lets you define an access scope—an origin, a destination, and optional intermediate components—and then it inspects security groups, NACLs, route tables, and gateways to report any potential paths that violate your scope. This is essential for proactive auditing and compliance. Second, Reachability Analyzer accepts a specific source and destination, plus protocol and port, and simulates the virtual network path to say whether the route is reachable and, if not, which component blocks it. Throughout this chapter you will see concrete examples, a CLI walkthrough for Reachability Analyzer, a hands-on lab to practice, and common mistakes to avoid such as relying on static analysis as if it were real-time traffic. By the end, you will know when to use each tool, how to interpret the findings, and how these tools reduce guesswork when troubleshooting multi-VPC and hybrid scenarios. Consider a recent connectivity issue you faced and how a static path analysis might have saved time.

We begin with clear objectives so you know what skills you'll leave with. First, you'll use Network Access Analyzer to audit network configurations against explicit access requirements. That means you will learn to define an access scope—an origin, destination, and optional intermediates—and interpret the analyzer's reported paths to detect unintended exposure. Second, you'll employ Reachability Analyzer to diagnose point-to-point connectivity problems. You'll learn to create a path analysis with the correct source and destination identifiers, choose protocol and port, and read the hop-by-hop results to identify blocking components. Both objectives focus on turning configuration state into actionable troubleshooting data rather than guessing from logs. Each objective includes a short practical checkpoint so you can verify competency: design a scope for a production subnet and run a basic reachability path between two ENIs. These skills are directly useful when operating multi-VPC, Transit Gateway, VPN, or Direct Connect networks where manual verification is time-consuming and error-prone.

This second objectives slide focuses on practice and interpretation. You will run a Reachability Analyzer path and read the explanation field to identify the exact blocking rule—this trains you to convert analyzer output to a remediation plan. You will also define at least one Network Access Analyzer scope to capture a real compliance requirement, for example preventing internet access to a production database subnet. Practically, this means setting an origin of '0.0.0.0/0' or 'All internet' and a destination subnet, then reviewing reported paths. Finally, you will learn to check IAM and cost implications before automating analyses. These steps are not theoretical: they prepare you to audit live environments and resolve connectivity failures faster than manual inspection. A common misconception we correct here is treating these tools as real-time traffic monitors—they analyze configuration state, not transient packets. That distinction guides when to use flow logs versus when to run a scope or path analysis.

When networks grow beyond a single VPC, manual troubleshooting becomes slow and error-prone. There are multiple places where access can be allowed or denied: security groups attached to ENIs, stateless NACLs on subnets, route table entries that forward traffic to an internet gateway, NAT gateway, or Transit Gateway, and peering or VPN links that connect networks. Each of these components must be examined and understood together. The problem is combinatorial: a single missing route or an overly broad security group can create either a silent failure or an unintended open path. Network Access Analyzer and Reachability Analyzer address different parts of this problem. Network Access Analyzer treats configuration as a whole and asks: given these current rules and routes, are there any potential paths that violate my policy? Reachability Analyzer answers a narrower question: given a source and destination, is there a path, and if not, which specific hop denies or lacks a rule? A common misconception is to rely only on flow logs or manual checks; flow logs show what happened, which is useful, but they may not reveal a potential misconfiguration that hasn't yet resulted in traffic. Translating debugging into declarative analysis lets you find issues earlier and with less guesswork. Think of manual checks as reading the symptoms, while these tools read the system's design and identify both symptoms and latent risks.

Network Access Analyzer inspects your network configuration to reveal potential paths that match a defined access scope. An access scope expresses the origin and destination you care about, plus optional intermediate constraints. For example, you might assert that ‘no internet access exists to production database subnets’ or that ‘only the management VPC may reach application management ports’. The analyzer then looks across security groups, NACLs, route tables, internet and NAT gateways, VPC peering, and Transit Gateways to enumerate any paths that would satisfy that scope. This is especially useful for compliance: rather than searching logs for traffic that happened, you check whether a configuration allows traffic at all. The workflow is: define scope, run analysis, review reported paths, and remediate misconfigurations. A common misconception is thinking the analyzer verifies live traffic; it does not. It reports potential paths based on current configuration. Use it to find latent exposures and to validate design constraints. As a concrete example, define a scope with origin: anywhere on the internet, destination: your DB subnet. If the analyzer reports a path, it will highlight the component—perhaps a route through an internet gateway combined with a permissive security group—that creates the exposure.

An access scope is the most important input to a Network Access Analyzer audit. Think of the scope as a filter that limits analysis to the traffic you care about. Start by choosing a clear origin: it can be an IP range, 'anywhere on the internet', or a specific VPC or subnet. Next, choose a precise destination: for compliance you might select a database subnet, specific ENIs, or a service endpoint. Optionally include intermediates such as Transit Gateways or specific VPC peering connections to narrow results. After you define the scope, run the analysis and inspect any returned paths. If you see many results, refine the scope—narrow the origin, constrain protocols or ports, or add an intermediate—to reduce noise. A practical example: to verify no internet access to your production DB subnet, set origin to the internet and destination to the DB subnet, then run analysis. If the analyzer finds a path, the report will show which combination of route entries and security group rules permit that path. Misdefining a scope is a common source of false negatives or noisy outputs; take time to iterate. The goal is to produce a focused report that directly points to misconfigurations you can fix.

Reachability Analyzer is designed for targeted troubleshooting: when you have a specific source and destination and want to know definitively whether a path exists and why. You provide the source and destination—these can be ENIs, IP addresses, or service endpoints—and optionally specify a protocol and destination port. The analyzer performs a static simulation of the virtual network path and returns either a reachable result or an explanation that identifies the blocking component. The value is precision: if the path is unreachable, the analysis tells you if a security group denied traffic, a route entry is missing, or a NACL blocks return traffic. Use it when two resources fail to communicate and you want to remove guesswork. A common use case is two EC2 instances in different subnets that cannot ping each other. Rather than manually examining every security group and route table, create a Reachability path and read the explanation. Remember that Reachability Analyzer works from the current configuration snapshot; if you modify rules after running an analysis, rerun to refresh results. This tool reduces troubleshooting time by directly mapping symptoms to a configuration-level cause.

The Reachability Analyzer can be invoked from the AWS CLI, which is useful for automating diagnostics or integrating with runbooks. The CLI flow typically creates a network-insights-path, starts an analysis, and then describes the analysis result. The create step requires a source IP or ENI ARN and a destination IP or ENI ARN, plus protocol and destination port when relevant. After you create the path, start the analysis and poll describe-network-insights-analyses until it reports success. The analysis output includes an Explanation field that states whether the path is reachable and, if not, precisely why. A concrete CLI example is included visually on this slide—use it as a pattern but replace ENI ARNs and IPs with your actual values. Remember IAM permissions: the calling principal needs CreateNetworkInsightsPath and Start/Describe permissions for the relevant resources. Also remember to re-run analyses after configuration changes to keep results current. A common mistake is reading the CLI output without checking the Explanation: that field is the actionable part that points to the blocking component. CLI example: creating a Reachability Analyzer path means create a path, start an analysis, and describe the analysis to read the explanation field for the blocking cause.. In practical terms, step through the aws cli commands to create and analyze a network-insights path. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The most valuable output from Reachability Analyzer is the hop-by-hop Explanation. It lists each virtual hop—source ENI, security groups, route table decisions, Transit Gateway attachments, NACL evaluations—and shows whether the hop accepted or denied traffic. When the analysis reports Reachable: Yes, you have verification that a path exists under current configuration. When it reports Reachable: No, examine the first denial in the explanation: it typically names the component and why it denied traffic, such as a security group without an inbound rule or a missing route entry. Translate that message into a remediation: add or adjust a security group rule, create or update a route table entry, or correct a NACL entry. Also verify return path symmetry: some components are stateful and some are not—if return traffic is blocked by a NACL, the forward path might appear allowed but the traffic still fails. A common misconception is assuming a reachability 'No' always points to a security group; the explanation may show a route or a missing Transit Gateway attachment instead. Use the explanation as your single source of truth when mapping to remediation.

These two tools solve different troubleshooting classes. Use Network Access Analyzer when you need a proactive, policy-driven audit across your network: define an access scope and find any potential paths that violate your requirements. It's best for compliance checks, audit runs, and broad validation across VPCs, Transit Gateways, and service endpoints. Reachability Analyzer is for targeted troubleshooting: when a specific connection fails, specify source and destination and get a hop-by-hop explanation that points to the blocking configuration. A helpful way to think about their difference is breadth versus depth—Network Access Analyzer covers broad surface area for unintended paths; Reachability Analyzer dives deep for one path and gives granular denial reasons. They complement each other: you might use Network Access Analyzer to find an exposure at scale, then use Reachability Analyzer to debug a particular affected pair. A common misconception is that one supersedes the other; they solve related but distinct problems and are often used together in a remediation workflow. Consider automating periodic Network Access Analyzer checks for compliance and using Reachability Analyzer in your incident runbook for targeted diagnostics.

This hands-on lab walks you through a common scenario: two EC2 instances initially communicate, then a security group change blocks ICMP and you use Reachability Analyzer to diagnose the cause. Start with two EC2 instances in the same VPC but different subnets. Verify initial connectivity by pinging the destination from the source instance. Next, edit the destination's security group and remove the inbound ICMP rule that allowed the source. Confirm the ping now fails. In the VPC console open Reachability Analyzer and create a path: choose the source ENI and destination ENI, set protocol to ICMP, and run the analysis. When completed, the analysis should show Reachable: No with an Explanation that names the security group denying ICMP. Remediate by re-adding the inbound ICMP rule referencing the source's security group, then run the analysis again. You should now see Reachable: Yes and the ping will succeed. This exercise demonstrates how Reachability Analyzer maps the symptom to the exact blocking component and shortens the repair loop compared to manual rule inspection. Before automating or delegating analyses, understand permissions, cost, and when to rerun checks. IAM: the principal performing analyses must have ec2:CreateNetworkInsightsPath, ec2:StartNetworkInsightsAnalysis, and ec2:Describe* permissions for the relevant resources. Apply least privilege—do not give broader rights than required for analysis. Cost: analyses are billed; be mindful when scheduling frequent automated runs—limit scope and frequency to balance assurance and cost. Safety: both tools perform read-only, static evaluations and do not change network configuration. That said, stale analysis results are a risk: if you change a security group or route after running an analysis, the prior result is no longer authoritative. Always rerun analyses after making configuration changes. Finally, combine analyzers with Flow Logs and CloudTrail: analyzers show potential or static path state, flow logs show actual observed traffic, and CloudTrail shows configuration changes over time. Using all three gives a robust troubleshooting and audit capability without over-relying on any single data source. Adopt a few best practices to make Network Access Analyzer and Reachability Analyzer effective parts of your network operations. First, be precise in scope definitions to reduce noise in Network Access Analyzer reports; iterative refinement yields actionable output. Second, use ENI identifiers for Reachability Analyzer when possible to avoid ambiguity introduced by changing IPs. Third, always check the Explanation field—it's the most actionable element and explicitly identifies the blocking component. Fourth, make analysis results part of your runbook: when an alarm fires, run a targeted Reachability analysis as a diagnostic step. Common mistakes include treating these tools as real-time traffic monitors, over-automating analyses without permission limits or cost controls, and failing to rerun analyses after configuration changes. Also avoid assuming the first reported path is the only important one; check whether multiple paths exist that could create exposure. Finally, combine findings with flow logs and CloudTrail records when validating an incident to ensure that both configuration and actual traffic behavior align. These practices will reduce mean time to repair and improve security posture. Let's summarize the most important concepts. First, Network Access Analyzer is a scope-driven tool for proactive auditing: you declare origins and destinations and it reports potential paths across security groups, NACLs, route tables, and gateways. Second, Reachability Analyzer performs point-to-point path analysis and gives a hop-by-hop Explanation naming the component that allows or denies traffic, which is invaluable for targeted troubleshooting. Third, both tools are static configuration analyses; they do not inspect live packet flows. Use them in combination with Flow Logs and CloudTrail for a complete troubleshooting and audit workflow. Remember to apply least privilege for permissions, watch cost when automating analyses, and rerun analyses after configuration changes to keep results accurate.
